column3: Sets a nearby affiliation boundary while naming both groups, qualifying any label-only reading.
Displays self-exaltation after clear signs as a contrary disposition to the focus's non-arrogance.
Adds merciful love and return as a mode of restored nearness.
Its comparative naming of Jews and polytheists supplies a cautionary parallel, though its concern is desire for life.
Frames the immediate passage's dispute over the Messiah and worship, without determining the relational comparison.
Links reverent fear with turning from rival authorities, a secondary parallel to humble disposition.
Adds enmity and hatred within a named group, resisting a simple label-wide account of relational distance.
Immediately precedes the focus with affiliation to disbelievers and its adverse consequence.
Contrasts fear directed toward people and toward God, a secondary lens on the focus's reverent posture.
Places Jews, Christians, and polytheists among several named communities while leaving final distinction to God.
Completes the preceding account of affiliation, directly setting up the focus's contrast.
Shows humility with hope and fear in responsive conduct, paralleling the stated absence of arrogance.
Shows reciprocal dismissal between Jews and Christians, complicating broad community labels.
Shows intimate bonds turning into enmity, clarifying that relational closeness is not fixed by name.
The bare presentation of a great sign adds little beyond a remote arrogance route.
Sets believing, socially weakened people against self-exalting elites, a social form of the focus's humility contrast.
Continues the immediate theological context but does not itself address the focus's social nearness.
Explicitly holds out affection between former enemies, making hostility and love changeable relations.
Contrasts directed loves and strongest love for God, supplying a broader frame for affection.
The wandering command does not materially illuminate the focus's relation or stated cause.
Defines a hostile relation in contrast to exclusive devotion, but remains broad.
Names claims associated with both Jews and Christians, providing surrounding doctrinal differentiation rather than a single group essence.
The brief denial and disobedience adds no distinct relational or humility evidence.
Links false claims and rejection of signs with arrogance, a secondary contrary pattern.
Contrasts exploitative learned and ascetic figures with the focus's priests and monks who do not exalt themselves.
Keeps repentance and forgiveness open in the immediate context, without explaining the comparison itself.
The demand for a particular sign offers little direct help with affection, enmity, or humility.
States that a community calling itself Christian can also have enmity and hatred placed among it, strongly qualifying label-based readings.
The command about entering the land has no clear added relation to the focus.
Near victory is not the social nearness described in the focus.
Contrasts the protective allegiance of believers with its absence for disbelievers.
Reassigns true greatness to God, forming a background contrast to human self-exaltation.
Its only supplied route is contrast evidence, and the text adds no clear focused relation.
Bases closest affiliation on following and faith rather than communal labels alone.
Further defines the immediate Messiah passage but does not itself explain affection or non-arrogance.
Specifies hostile conduct and a wish for disbelief, a useful counterpart to the later possibility of affection.
The repudiation of alleged partners does not add a focused social or humility connection.
Covenant and obedience provide background context but little direct explanation of the focus.
Reverent fear is only a remote and tentative parallel to the stated disposition.
Contrasts fear of people with fear of God, clarifying a possible contrary direction for reverence.
Pairs human arrogance with tireless worship nearby to God, though this repeats the humility contrast.
The supplied link is contrast-only and the text does not add a specific focused relation.
Makes acceptance conditional on following a way, qualifying simple expectations of intercommunity approval.
The immediate warning against powerless objects is only peripheral to the focus's relation.
Shows divided responses around Jesus and support against enemies, a limited contextual parallel.
The summons concerning alleged partners adds no distinct help with the focus.
Forbids hostility from becoming transgression, providing an ethical boundary for enmity.
Fear and a sign are a distant, non-social parallel to the focus's secondary reading.
Makes self-exaltation a response to monotheistic proclamation, a repeated contrary disposition.
Links recited signs, arrogance, and wrongdoing, reinforcing but not extending the contrast.
Gives affection and mercy a concrete relation-forming role, directly enriching the focus's mawadah.
Embodies faith as prostration and explicitly not self-exalting, directly clarifying the focus's stated cause.
Continues the immediate warning against excess and misguidance, offering contextual restraint.
A wish for mutual softening is not clearly the affection praised in the focus.
Support for messengers and believers adds little to the relational comparison.
Adds covenant breach, hardened hearts, and pardon in the same surah, supplying a nuanced nearby background for the named contrast.
Connects knowing enemies with proper protective allegiance, a broad relational frame.
Separation from alleged partners does not materially explain the focus.
Praise of God offers only an indirect background to the arrogance contrast.
Joins guidance and mercy to reverent fear, a secondary parallel to humility.
Defines nearness to the Lord through worship without arrogance, directly clarifying the focus's causal language.
Supplies the immediate account of disobedience and transgression before the focus's comparison.
The name associated with affection is too remote from the focus's social affection.
Challenges competing Jewish and Christian identity claims, qualifying labels as sufficient guides.
Shared food and permitted marriage across communities offer concrete proximity that tempers a simple distance reading.
Shows self-exaltation bound to denial of return, a repeated contrary disposition.
Return to the Lord is too general to add to the focus.
Locates grandeur with God, supplying a broad counterpoint to human arrogance.
Frames enmity as opposition to God, angels, and messengers, distinguishing a relational stance from a mere label.
Those near God do not disdain worship, a concise parallel to non-arrogance.
Continues the immediate critique through failure to restrain wrongdoing.
Makes affection a result granted to faithful, righteous people, directly supporting conduct-linked closeness.
Contests retrospective Jewish and Christian labels, reinforcing caution about identity claims.
False recourse to a distant harm-bringing patron does not clearly illuminate the focus.
Describes divine nearness and response, a secondary but distinct sense of closeness.
Shows aggression and inconsistent commitment within a named community, further resisting group-essential readings.
Immediately follows the focus by showing recognition, tears, and faith, directly displaying the responsive people described.
Shows arrogance defending rejection of what others believe, repeating the social mechanism.
Shows followers confronting self-exalting leaders, extending arrogance into social responsibility.
Nearness here is capture without escape, not the focus's relational nearness.
Pairs forgiveness and love, but remains a generic and already-covered affection parallel.
Challenges exclusive Jewish or Christian claims, qualifying label-based conclusions.
Immediately continues the described group's faith response and hope of joining the righteous.
Presents refusal to prostrate through arrogance as the archetypal opposite of the focus's non-arrogance.
Universal prostration without arrogance reinforces the humility side of the contrast.
Places mutual enmity alongside guidance, distinguishing hostility from the offered route of direction.
Near divine help is not the social nearness in the focus.
False attributions and promised reward add no distinct focused connection.
Concludes the immediate response with reward, completing the displayed outcome of the focus's nearer group.
Joins turning away with self-exaltation, a concise but redundant contrary pattern.
Shows varied response and manipulation among some from a named community, further cautioning against uniform labels.
Near opening after allegiance is not the focus's social closeness.
Recalls a group's intended violence and restraint of it, a limited nearby instance of hostility.
Places arrogance after received signs and denial, reinforcing the focus's contrary disposition.
Falsehood and denial are too broad to add a distinct relation to the focus.
Sets a boundary on affection toward active opposition to God and the messenger, sharply qualifying the focus's praise of closeness.
Mutual waiting adds no identifiable relation to the focus.
Shows deference to social magnates leading astray, extending the risks of elevated human status.
Prideful display and obstruction are only a distant arrogance parallel.
Depicts turning away from forgiveness while self-exalting, a concise but redundant contrary case.
Places believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians under shared criteria of faith and righteous action, sharply limiting label-only conclusions.
Offers a common orientation to the People of the Book, a counterpoint to treating distance as the sole relation.
Explicitly says the People of the Book are not all alike and identifies a worshipping group among them.
Specifies faith, right action, and haste toward good as marks of the upright group, supplying conduct-based differentiation.
Describes some People of the Book as believing, humble before God, and not trading signs for gain; it closely parallels the focus's exception.
Warns believers against seeking might through allegiance to disbelievers, clarifying a different sense of relational proximity.
Names the Messiah among those who do not disdain service to God, directly paralleling the focus's non-arrogance beside the Christian reference.
Pairs faith and righteous action with mercy and bounty, extending the outcome of humble response.
Addresses the people of the Gospel as responsible to what God revealed therein, adding immediate community-specific context.
Combines distinct communities with a shared call to compete in good works, qualifying categorical comparison.
Forbids taking religious mockers as allies, directly distinguishing hostile conduct from mere communal naming.
Frames resentment from some People of the Book around belief in God and revelation, adding a possible hostile stance without universalizing it.
Names rabbis and learned figures who fail to restrain sinful speech and consumption, a needed contrary reading beside the focus's priests and monks.
Describes a moderate community among the People of the Book, directly supporting internal differentiation.
Addresses the People of the Book through standing by Torah, Gospel, and what was sent down, making religious conduct rather than label consequential.
Again places believers, Jews, Sabians, and Christians under shared faith and righteous-action criteria.
Provides the immediate contrary conclusion for denial and rejection of signs, completing the focus's following sequence.
Forbids reciprocal insult across worship commitments lest hostility produce abuse of God, setting a boundary on adversarial relations.
Requires receptivity to peace when an opposing party inclines to it, showing enmity is not the only available relation.
Names conflict with some People of the Book in a specific political-religious frame, a necessary contrary context that should not be generalized.
Shows rabbis and monks being taken as lords, a significant contrary account of religious roles beside the focus's favorable description.
Links hidden and open knowledge of God with rejection of the self-exalting, reinforcing the stated causal contrast.
Describes those above as fearing their Lord and doing what they are commanded, a secondary reverence parallel.
Forbids proud bearing and denies human capacity for self-greatness, a broad contrary posture.
Commands patient companionship with those who call on their Lord, reinforcing humble, non-status-based closeness.
Connects ritual devotion with humility before God, a secondary parallel to the focus's disposition.
Places arrogance among elites as a response to a messenger, extending the social form of the focus's contrast.
Defines servants of the Merciful by walking humbly and answering ignorant address with peace, directly joining humility to social conduct.
Names denial despite inward certainty as wrongdoing and self-exaltation, a contrary response to recognized truth.
Reserves the final abode for those who do not seek exaltation or corruption on earth, directly stating the contrary of the focus's cause.
Commands the best manner of discourse with the People of the Book while retaining an exception for wrongdoing, closely qualifying relational distance.
Forbids turning the cheek from people and walking exultantly, connecting arrogance to interpersonal manner.
Rejects taking other protectors on the claim that they bring nearness to God, distinguishing false religious proximity from the focus's social closeness.
Associates disputation without warrant with pride in the hearts of those who do it, a repeated contrary pattern.
Links unwarranted disputation and arrogance, adding a further contrary route without resolving its social scope.
Displays a people self-exalting on earth and claiming superior strength, a collective form of the focus's contrary disposition.
Pairs firmness toward deniers with mercy among believers and bodily marks of worship, giving a differentiated relational and humble profile.
Makes peoples and tribes occasions for mutual knowing and assigns honor to God-consciousness, strongly resisting essentialized group rank.
Places compassion and mercy among followers of Jesus while also preserving a contrary account of later monastic innovation.
Describes later believers praying for predecessors and lacking rancor toward believers, a direct positive model of communal affection.
Permits kindness and justice toward those who neither fight nor expel, sharply distinguishing non-hostility from active enmity.
Restricts the prohibition of alliance to those who fight, expel, or support expulsion, providing the key boundary for 60:7 and the focus.
